title: Break and recover HELICOIL tangs from an ODRI actuator shell
objective: Finish four already-installed M2.5 × 3.75 mm HELICOIL inserts in a representative ODRI actuator shell base: coaxially place a straight tang break-off mandrel, strike it with a separately manipulated hammer to fracture each tang at its notch, then recover every free fragment without damaging or displacing the inserts or shell.
skills: precision grasping of a narrow mandrel
coaxial insertion into recessed M2.5 inserts
bimanual mandrel stabilization and controlled hammering
success_conditions: Full success requires four contact-loaded notch fractures, four freely moving tang fragments deposited in the recovery tray, no fragment remaining in the shell cavity, every insert retained within frozen pose tolerances, no shell/coil damage, and a two-second hands-off hold. Partial credit covers safe alignment or fewer than four completed fractures when every released fragment remains contained. Failure includes an unrecovered fragment, off-axis overload, insert displacement, shell damage, tool jamming, or fragment escape. Pose/velocity writes, waypoint-triggered fracture, permanent grasp welds, fixed fragments, or manufactured collision suppression invalidate the attempt. Initial prototype assumptions—0.55 mm wire diameter, 1.8 mm tang chord, 18 N equivalent axial break threshold over a 20 ms window, and 8 N radial-damage threshold—are explicitly uncalibrated and must be frozen before native testing.
industrial_value: The pinned ODRI robot-actuator preparation procedure expressly requires four M2.5 × 3.75 mm inserts in the shell base, removal with a tang break-off tool, and no tangs left inside the part. Manufacturer documentation identifies the notch as the predetermined fracture location and provides a size-matched M2.5 straight mandrel.
dexterity: The robot must preserve coaxial alignment in a roughly 2.6 mm insert crest opening while another hand delivers a controlled impact, avoid loading the surrounding printed boss, withdraw the tool, and recover small free debris from a cavity. Bimanual use is grounded in the manufacturer diagram showing one hand holding the straight mandrel while a hammer strikes it; it is not imposed on the alternative spring-loaded tool mechanism.

asset_plan: Use an independently authored representative shell-base fixture, not an exact-product claim. Ground it in the inspected pinned ODRI images: four marked M2.5 bosses are distributed around the open shell-base cavity; the installation photograph shows vertical tool access to a perimeter boss; the completed-shell photograph confirms the cavity, large through-openings, boss heights, and fragment escape paths. Anchor scale with the documented M2.5 × 3.75 mm insert, 2.60 mm crest diameter, four-hole count, and 160 mm actuator-module segment length. Model each retained coil proxy and its separate tang at the visually verified notch anatomy. Use a representative straight M2.5 mandrel corresponding to item 0158 040 1000 and hammer actuation matching Böllhoff page-17 diagram h; do not mix it with the TB-M spring tool. Disclose all unsourced handle dimensions. Before robot integration, verify native PhysX axial-impact fracture, insufficient-energy and glancing-blow controls, off-axis damage, wrong-hole strikes, coil retention, free-fragment collision/containment, reset freshness, substep force/impulse/energy logging, and timestep convergence using retained PRE/POST PhysxManager callback handles. Reject or revise the assumptions if stable contact coupling is not demonstrated.
risk: The closest prior families include nail hammering, automatic center-punch use, pop-rivet stem disposal, panel/tile fracture, and slide-hammer extraction. Novelty depends on the combined installed-insert access, bimanual alignment-preserving impulse, preservation of a functional coil in a robot shell, and mandatory recovery of every internal fragment—not on debris or industrial naming alone. Exact notch strength and tool-handle dimensions remain prototype assumptions, but the essential retention, fracture location, actuation mode, insert size, access orientation, shell cavity, and required fragment outcome are evidenced.
